analysis.one_liner: Makes online marketplaces legally responsible for counterfeit goods that threaten health and safety sold on their sites.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee 30–8 with bipartisan support, but never received a vote by the full House and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The SHOP SAFE Act would have made online marketplaces legally responsible when third-party sellers use their platforms to sell counterfeits of products that can hurt people — like fake medicine, car parts, or children's items. A platform could avoid being sued only by checking sellers' identities, requiring US-based contacts for legal service, screening listings for fakes before they go up, quickly removing reported counterfeits, and banning repeat offenders. It also penalized brand owners who knowingly filed fake takedown claims to knock competitors off a site. The bill passed the House Judiciary Committee 30–8 with votes from both parties, but was never brought to the House floor and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who shop on third-party online marketplaces would face fewer fake medicines, electronics, toys, and auto parts that can injure or poison them, since platforms would have to verify sellers, screen listings, and remove repeat counterfeiters or face lawsuits. Legitimate brand owners would gain a new legal tool to force platforms to act. Honest small sellers would also gain some protection, because the bill lets them collect damages of $2,500–$75,000 per notice when a brand owner knowingly files a false counterfeit complaint that gets their listing removed.

how_it_helps.text: Makes online marketplaces legally responsible for counterfeit goods affecting health and safety unless they verify sellers, screen listings proactively, remove flagged fakes, and ban repeat offenders.
Requires platforms to display each seller's verified identity, location, and the country the goods shipped from, so shoppers can see who they are actually buying from.
Counterbalances platform duties with penalties for brand owners who knowingly file false takedown claims against sellers, with damages of $2,500 to $75,000 per improper notice.

analysis.who_pays: Online marketplaces like Amazon and eBay, which would bear the cost of verifying sellers, proactively screening listings, and removing counterfeits, and could face contributory liability suits if they do not. Some of that cost would likely be passed on to sellers and shoppers through higher fees and prices, and small sellers would face more paperwork to stay on the platforms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Online marketplaces and their third-party sellers

drawbacks.text: The compliance duties — verified seller identities, registered agents, proactive screening, accurate images, and repeat-offender bans — will cost platforms money, and some of that cost is likely to be passed on to consumers through fees and prices.

Liability attaches before the platform can easily know a listing is counterfeit, and while the bill scales duties to platform size, small and mid-sized marketplaces face proportionally heavier compliance burdens than giants like Amazon.

Statutory damages of $2,500–$75,000 per improper takedown notice create a litigation deterrent that could make brand owners more cautious about legitimate enforcement, potentially letting some counterfeits stay up longer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is reasonable: platforms that meet defined screening duties are safe from suit, and liability attaches only to health-and-safety goods, so the burden falls on categories where counterfeits genuinely hurt people — fake medicines, auto parts, and children's products. The takedown-abuse safeguards (liability for knowing misrepresentations, and 10-notice thresholds before small platforms are covered) are a real good-faith concession to sellers and platforms, not window dressing. The honest costs are real: compliance is easier for large platforms than small ones, seller onboarding will get slower, and some compliance costs will reach consumers through prices. It is a genuinely consumer-protective bill, though its litigation machinery favors well-resourced brand owners most.

outcome.mechanism: It passed out of the House Judiciary Committee 30–8 but the full House never voted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Introduced September 26, 2021, the bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, whose chairman, Jerrold Nadler, was also its lead sponsor.

Three days later, on September 29, 2021, the committee met, marked the bill up, and ordered it reported with a substitute amendment by a vote of 30–8 — a strong bipartisan showing for a consumer-protection measure.
Despite that vote, the bill never received a vote by the full House and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online marketplaces that sell third-party goods keep the existing liability rules and face no new duty to screen out counterfeit health and safety products; counterfeit sellers keep the market open to them.

for.name: Jerrold Nadler

for.name: Darrell Issa, Hank Johnson, and Ben Cline
for.role: Original cosponsors across both parties on the Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship.

for.what_they_did: Voted 30–8 to order the bill reported to the full House.

against.name: Large online marketplaces and e-commerce trade associations
against.role: Amazon, eBay, and allied industry groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill's new platform liability for third-party counterfeits.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — Democrat Jerrold Nadler with Republican Darrell Issa and two other members — and the committee reported it 30–8 with members of both parties on each side.

industries.industry: Third-party e-commerce marketplaces (Amazon, eBay, and similar platforms)
industries.note: The bill would impose a 13-point verification, screening, and removal regime backed by trademark liability, raising operating costs, particularly for seller verification and proactive screening. Platforms also gain a new tool to sue abusive takedown filers.
The bill gives them a direct legal claim against platforms that host counterfeit versions of their goods, strengthening enforcement they currently must pursue seller by seller.

industries.industry: Small third-party sellers on online marketplaces
industries.note: Legitimate small sellers benefit from fewer counterfeit competitors but face new verification, attestation, and identity-display requirements; sellers falsely accused of counterfeiting gain statutory damages for improper takedowns.
